articles.title: Entenda projeto aprovado no Senado que cria regras para exploração de terras raras e outras riquezas minerais brasileiras | G1
articles.standfirst: A Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos prevê um incentivo de R$ 7 bilhões para o setor.
articles.summary: A Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos prevê um incentivo de R$ 7 bilhões para o setor.
articles.body:
Entenda projeto aprovado no Senado que cria regras para exploração de terras raras e outras riquezas minerais brasileiras — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

O Senado aprovou nesta semana o projeto que cria a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos . Entre eles, estão as terras raras .

O projeto cria regras para a exploração de algumas das mais importantes riquezas minerais do Brasil. É o caso do lítio - usado na fabricação de baterias de celular e de carros elétricos. Ou o nióbio , fundamental para a produção de ligas metálicas mais resistentes e de produtos aeroespaciais.

Vale também para as terras raras , conjunto de 17 elementos considerados estratégicos para vários setores da economia. Como as indústrias de smartphones, equipamentos eólicos, drones. É longa a lista de produtos feitos a partir das terras raras, matéria-prima abundante no Brasil, que possui a segunda maior reserva do mundo, atrás apenas da China.

Pelas novas regras, que ainda precisam ser sancionadas pela Presidência da República, serão destinados R$ 5 bilhões em créditos tributários para as empresas do setor mineral. O projeto também cria um fundo garantidor, com recursos federais de até R$ 2 bilhões para financiar os negócios.

Desde a retirada desses minérios da natureza até que se transformem em produtos industrializados, são várias etapas. As empresas que investirem no beneficiamento desses minerais críticos e estratégicos aqui no Brasil terão acesso a linhas de financiamento com condições mais vantajosas. O objetivo da lei é evitar que o país seja apenas um grande exportador de matéria-prima e possa desenvolver produtos com maior valor de mercado.

Um outro fundo, com recursos das próprias mineradoras, vai financiar pesquisa e desenvolvimento de novas tecnologias.

"Hoje, pesquisa e tecnologia, principalmente pensando em aplicação, são um investimento de risco. Elas precisam desse apoio para que elas consigam desenvolver a tecnologia”, afirma André Pimenta, coordenador do Laboratório de Terras Raras da FIEMG.

O projeto de lei estabelece ainda a criação de um conselho nacional que ficará encarregado de aprovar fusões, aquisições, entrada de capital estrangeiro e outros movimentos de mercado. A maior parte dos integrantes desse conselho será do governo federal , o que preocupa alguns representantes das mineradoras, que temem mudanças de rumo em projetos de longo prazo.

"É muito importante nós, como país, encontrarmos o equilíbrio que significa como a gente garante segurança para as pessoas, segurança para o país, mas garante também a continuidade desses fluxos de financiamento, que continuam sendo o grande desafio do setor”, diz Pablo Cesário, presidente do Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração.
tags: Laboratório de Terras Raras da FIEMG

articles.title: Trump faces down beef backlash. Will import plan pay off?
articles.summary: President Trump is pushing ahead with his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans, despite the backlash from cattle farmers and R...
articles.body:
President Trump is pushing ahead with his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans, despite the backlash from cattle farmers and Republicans whose states would be most be most affected.

In an apparent effort to soften the blow, Trump signed executive orders Friday, including one that allows ranchers and farmers to process and package their own products, and another that promotes country-of-origin labeling across all foreign beef, which would require congressional action.

Justin Tupper, president of the United States Cattlemen's Association, said it appreciated the new orders but remained "cautious on what comes next."

Following the signings in the Oval Office, Trump sought to play down the impact of his beef import plan, telling reporters, "We're doing it in a very limited fashion because our ranchers can handle it," adding, "Our ranchers want the prices to be down too."

When announcing the move last month to import 300,000 metric tons of beef without tariffs for 90 days, Trump said the beef would be sold at 25 percent below current market prices. He revealed for the first time Friday the beef would be coming primarily from Brazil and Argentina.

Those critical of the move say it will barely move the needle on Americans' cost-of-living concerns, while forcing a key part of Trump's base to pay a heavy price.

"Trump is right to address the issue of beef prices but stepped in it in doing so in a way that parts of his base are going to react to," said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist.

"The administration — and Trump in particular — need to be spending all their efforts on lowering prices across the board, including the latest cost driver, Iran," he added.

Glynn Tonsor, an assistant professor in the Kansas State University Department of Agricultural Economics, said the odds of this deal lowering prices and helping ranchers "are about zero."

"If there's something that reduces beef prices for consumers, by definition, that reduces the dollars going back into the industry, because the price clearing the market for retail beef is lower, and therefore one has to pause and say, is that good for producers?" he said. "So, there's a world where one or the other might happen, but I don't see any world where both could happen out of the same announcement."

The 300,000 metric ton figure only represents about a 2 percent increase in beef supply, Tonsor noted.

"I'm on record saying it'll have very, very small, if any, impact on the price that consumers pay for beef," he said.

Beef prices have been soaring across the country. The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. is roughly $6.89, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis .

The prices have gone up because the U.S. is raising record-low cattle numbers due to several factors, including droughts and rising operational costs, all the while demand remains high.

Data from the Department of Agriculture showed that the U.S started with 86.2 million cattle at the beginning of the year, the lowest cattle inventory since 1951 .

Affordability, meanwhile, remains a top issue for voters ahead of the midterms. Trump captured 62 percent of the rural vote in 2024, but his approval among that voter group has fallen from July to August, according to polls done by ActiVote .

The cattle industry and GOP lawmakers argue that lowering prices for Americans shouldn't come at the cost of America's ranchers.

"While America's cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd," Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, said in a statement.

"This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds," he added, saying the import plan throws "cold water" on the investment necessary to expand herds.

David Anderson, a professor and extension specialist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University, said the markets should have been left to work themselves out.

"You have to have cattle producers that are profitable to get that market signal to expand, to increase beef production which then brings down prices," Anderson said. "And so, we finally have prices that are profitable and something like this gets announced."

He said it comes at a bad time when ranchers are making decisions about their herds.

"This was just another announcement, another thing hitting the market to drive down prices," he said. "Lowering prices reduces that incentive to expand."

Several Republican lawmakers have spoken out too. Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and Jerry Moran (Kan.), Rep. Adrian Smith (Neb.) and 50 others wrote a letter to Trump urging him to prioritize policies that would help ranchers.

"Cattle markets are cyclical, and ranchers use the upswings to prepare for the inevitable downturn," the lawmakers wrote. "Any intervention in the natural system, especially at a time when producers are making marketing decisions, threatens to pick winners and losers and undermine the long-term viability of family-owned cattle operations throughout the supply chain."

A report from The Wall Street Journal earlier this past week said that Trump met with Joesley Batista, who shares control of JBS, the world's largest meatpacker, in the Oval Office a day before he made the announcement.

The sources said that during the meeting, Batista lobbied Trump to drop the import tax as a way to mitigate costs of beef for consumers.

In response to the report, the White House said Trump's "action to address a short-term supply crunch in the beef market was the result of a long policy planning and coordination process involving domestic stakeholders; this action was not done as the result of any one conversation."

Brandon Scholz, a former Republican turned independent political analyst from Wisconsin, said Trump's move gives a "false sense of hope to consumers … and then we're going to start losing our producers and our growers."

"I think he's just putting out a false sense of security in front of the midterms," Scholz said. "I simply can't imagine that this is something that people are going to go to the voting booth and go, 'You know, that was really great that Trump got us all that cheap beef.'"

articles.title: Por que o acordo de US$ 18 bilhões da Meta importa além dos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Acordo que impõe limites ao uso do Facebook e do Instagram por adolescentes pode servir de referência para outros países, incluindo o Brasil, que também ampliam a pressão sobre as redes sociais.
articles.summary: Acordo que impõe limites ao uso do Facebook e do Instagram por adolescentes pode servir de referência para outros países, incluindo o Brasil.
articles.body:
Há bons motivos para ser cético quanto ao impacto que o mais recente acordo legal da Meta terá sobre a gigante de tecnologia. A empresa já sobreviveu a escândalos, audiências no Congresso e multas regulatórias sem grandes danos duradouros.

Um acordo aprovado pelo tribunal no valor de até US$ 18 bilhões parece enorme , mas a Meta pode arcar com isso: o valor equivale a cerca de 8,5% da receita total da empresa em 2025.

A grande questão não é o dinheiro. É que os governos estão começando a regular como as plataformas de mídia social são construídas.

O acordo pode marcar uma mudança importante na política de redes sociais justamente porque trata da estrutura das próprias plataformas e exige que as empresas façam mudanças para proteger crianças.

Algoritmos de recomendação, rolagem infinita, falta de controles de idade e outros recursos projetados para prender a atenção estão cada vez mais sob escrutínio. Os governos começam a intervir não apenas no conteúdo oferecido pelas plataformas, mas também na forma como os produtos são projetados e funcionam.

E essa mudança vai além dos Estados Unidos. Em vários países — especialmente no Brasil — os governos estão dispostos a enfrentar empresas de tecnologia nos tribunais para promover mudanças.

O litígio surgiu de um caso federal movido por dezenas de estados, com Califórnia, Colorado, Kentucky e Nova Jersey levando suas reivindicações de proteção ao consumidor a julgamento. A Meta nega qualquer irregularidade.

Segundo um acordo aprovado por um juiz federal em 26 de agosto de 2026, a empresa concordou com mudanças para usuários menores de 18 anos, incluindo um limite padrão de duas horas diárias combinadas entre Facebook e Instagram, restrições ao uso entre meia-noite e 6h, controles mais rígidos nas notificações e verificações de idade mais rigorosas. Um auditor independente supervisionará o cumprimento das medidas.

As defesas legais da indústria de mídias sociais há muito se apoiam na Seção 230, a lei federal que geralmente impede que plataformas sejam tratadas como responsáveis pelo conteúdo de terceiros.

Os casos contra a Meta e outras empresas, muitos dos quais ainda estão em andamento, investigam uma questão diferente. Os autores argumentam que alguns danos surgem de características criadas pelas próprias plataformas.

No início deste mês, o 9º Circuito rejeitou a tentativa de Meta e TikTok de recorrer das decisões que permitiam que milhares de processos prosseguissem.

A decisão foi restrita: o tribunal disse que a Seção 230 oferece uma defesa contra responsabilidade, e não imunidade contra processos. Em outras palavras, não decidiu se Meta e TikTok eram responsáveis, apenas que as empresas não conseguiram impedir os casos nessa fase.

Em 7 de agosto, um tribunal do Novo México também emitiu uma sentença final, reduzindo a responsabilidade financeira total da Meta no estado para US$ 942 milhões e impondo cinco anos de mudanças supervisionadas pelo tribunal no Facebook e Instagram para usuários do estado.

As medidas incluem verificação de idade mais rigorosa, limites de tempo e restrições a recursos voltados para usuários jovens. A corte também rejeitou o argumento da Meta de que proteções federais para plataformas online a protegiam da responsabilidade pelos produtos que projetou. A Meta está contestando a decisão.

O acordo de US$ 17 bilhões, portanto, acompanha uma mudança jurídica mais ampla: os tribunais estão começando a testar a ideia de que as plataformas podem ser responsabilizadas não apenas pelo conteúdo publicado pelos usuários, mas também por elementos dos produtos que desenvolvem.

A Meta aceitou que controles sobre tempo online, notificações, verificação de idade e sistemas de recomendação podem funcionar em plataformas que atendem centenas de milhões de pessoas. Isso dificulta que Roblox, Snap, TikTok, YouTube e outros concorrentes argumentem que salvaguardas semelhantes são tecnicamente impossíveis.

Existem limites óbvios para o acordo. Duas horas por dia dificilmente representam abstinência digital. Pais podem anular os controles, e adolescentes conseguem contornar algumas restrições. A verificação de idade continua tecnicamente difícil e também levanta preocupações de privacidade. Ainda não se sabe se essas mudanças vão melhorar a saúde mental dos adolescentes.

Mesmo assim, o acordo vai além das promessas conhecidas da indústria de "fazer melhor". Os reguladores estão começando a interferir no próprio produto.

As consequências financeiras de longo prazo também podem ser maiores do que a cifra principal sugere. A Meta eliminou uma grande fonte de incerteza jurídica, o que os investidores inicialmente pareciam receber bem.

No entanto, milhares de casos envolvendo indivíduos e distritos escolares continuam. Mais importante para o modelo de negócio, restrições em notificações, recomendações e tempo online podem reduzir a atenção da qual dependem as receitas publicitárias.

Cerca de 30% do compromisso financeiro máximo da Meta depende da adoção de salvaguardas semelhantes pelo TikTok e pelo YouTube, com pagamentos equivalentes. A Meta tem interesse em garantir que as restrições no Instagram não façam os jovens simplesmente migrarem para concorrentes.

Se TikTok e YouTube aderirem ao acordo, a Meta se comprometeu a endurecer ainda mais suas próprias regras, reduzindo o limite diário para uma hora por aplicativo e ampliando as restrições noturnas das 22h às 7h.

A segurança infantil é uma das poucas questões tecnológicas com apoio bipartidário em Washington. Câmara e Senado discutem leis que imporiam novas obrigações às plataformas. Em junho, a Câmara aprovou a Lei de Segurança Online para Crianças e, em 5 de agosto, o Comitê de Comércio do Senado avançou com a legislação.

No fim de agosto, senadores também citaram o acordo com a Meta ao retomar a iniciativa pela Kids Off Social Media Act.

As consequências do acordo da Meta provavelmente vão além dos Estados Unidos . Reguladores de outros países já seguem uma direção semelhante. Em julho, a Comissão Europeia concluiu preliminarmente que a Meta violou a Lei de Serviços Digitais devido ao design viciante do Facebook e do Instagram.

A investigação destacou rolagem infinita, reprodução automática e algoritmos que personalizam o que os usuários veem.

A Lei de Segurança Online do Reino Unido impõe deveres de segurança infantil às plataformas. A Austrália exige que as plataformas tomem medidas para impedir que crianças menores de 16 anos mantenham contas em redes sociais.

O Brasil colocou muitos desses princípios em lei . A ECA Digital, em vigor desde 17 de março, estabelece novas obrigações para plataformas digitais usadas por crianças e adolescentes brasileiros, mesmo quando o provedor está no exterior.

A lei exige verificação de idade, proteções padrão mais fortes e ferramentas de supervisão parental. Contas de usuários de até 16 anos devem ser vinculadas a um adulto responsável.

As regras brasileiras também miram características associadas ao uso excessivo ou compulsivo. Um decreto que regulamenta a lei restringe recursos como rolagem infinita, reprodução automática e notificações destinadas a prolongar o engajamento.

As famílias devem receber ferramentas para monitorar e limitar o uso, enquanto as configurações padrão para usuários mais jovens devem oferecer maior proteção.

Por isso, os compromissos da Meta no acordo importam para o Brasil menos como precedente legal e mais como demonstração do que é tecnicamente possível. As autoridades brasileiras já têm poder legal para exigir proteções mais fortes.

Se a empresa concordou em impor restrições noturnas e reduzir as notificações para adolescentes na Califórnia ou em Nova York, as autoridades brasileiras podem perguntar por que proteções semelhantes deveriam ser mais fracas no país.

O Brasil também possui ferramentas de fiscalização. A ANPD — o órgão brasileiro responsável pela proteção de dados — já começou a examinar sistemas de verificação de idade operados por Apple, Google e Microsoft. Em 21 de agosto, a fiscalização foi ampliada para mais de 20 outras plataformas, incluindo ChatGPT, Claude, Discord, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, X e YouTube.

Em 25 de agosto, a ANPD multou a ByteDance em aproximadamente US$ 31 milhões por violações da lei brasileira de proteção de dados envolvendo crianças e adolescentes. Também ordenou que o TikTok excluísse dados que, segundo o órgão, foram coletados de forma inadequada e exigiu que a empresa apresentasse um plano de conformidade.

Um novo caso envolvendo o Discord pode mostrar até onde o Brasil está disposto a ir para obrigar empresas de tecnologia a cumprir as novas regras.

Em 12 de agosto, a ANPD ordenou que a plataforma sediada nos EUA suspendesse as funções de transmissão ao vivo e compartilhamento de vídeos no Brasil até que pudesse demonstrar salvaguardas adequadas para crianças e adolescentes. A medida ocorreu após o caso de suicídio de uma menina de 13 anos no Brasil, em julho, que foi ligado pelas autoridades à plataforma.

O governo brasileiro ampliou a disputa em 25 de agosto, quando o Gabinete do Procurador-Geral entrou com uma ação civil buscando o equivalente a US$ 100 milhões em indenização coletiva e ordens judiciais para que o Discord mude suas práticas.

Entre as demandas estão verificação de idade mais rigorosa, supervisão parental, configurações padrão mais seguras, interrupção em tempo real de conteúdos seriamente prejudiciais e medidas para impedir que servidores banidos simplesmente reapareçam com novos nomes. O governo afirma que não busca fechar o serviço.

O Discord contestou as medidas, argumentando que são desproporcionais e questionando a autoridade do regulador para impô-las. Em 2 de setembro, um juiz federal deu ao Discord 10 dias para apresentar uma nova proposta de proteção aos usuários.

A disputa brasileira se sobrepõe diretamente a questões que estão sendo discutidas nos Estados Unidos. Nos dois países, as autoridades estão recorrendo à verificação de idade, às configurações padrão e a outras decisões de design que antes eram, em grande parte, deixadas para as próprias empresas de tecnologia.

O Brasil pode se tornar um teste importante para saber se leis ambiciosas de segurança infantil podem ser aplicadas sem enfraquecer proteções legais básicas.

articles.title: Quaest mostra o que mais pesa para o eleitor no voto para presidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada neste domingo (6) aponta quais são as características do candidato que os eleitores consideram ser as mais importantes na decisão do voto para presidente.
articles.summary: Pesquisa aponta quais são as características do candidato que os eleitores consideram ser as mais importantes na decisão do voto.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada neste domingo (6) aponta quais são as características do candidato que os eleitores consideram ser as mais importantes na decisão do voto para presidente. O levantamento foi encomendado pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo.

31% dos entrevistados citam não estar envolvido com corrupção .

para 28%, o mais importante é ter compromisso com a democracia .

15% respoderam que é ser duro no combate à violência e ao crime .

apenas 2% citaram a opção ser crítico ao STF .

Ser duro no combate à violência e ao crime: 15%

Quaest: características mais importantes para decidir votar em um candidato a presidente — Foto: Arte/g1

Na divisão do eleitorado por posicionamento político, 33% dos eleitores independentes citaram o não envolvimento com a corrupção como o fator mais importante, e 26% citaram a defesa da democracia.

Há uma diferença entre lulistas e bolsonaristas. Entre os primeiros, a característica mais mencionada (29%) foi o compromisso com a democracia. Já no grupo bolsonarista, 41% consideram que é essencial o candidato não ter ligações com casos de corrupção. Veja o detalhamento no gráfico abaixo:

Quaest: característica mais importante para decidir voto para presidente por identificação política — Foto: Arte/g1

A Quaest perguntou também aos eleitores qual característica é a mais importante para não votar de jeito nenhum em um candidato. Veja as respostas:

Não ter compromisso com a democracia: 21%

Ser fraco no combate à violência e ao crime: 13%

Quaest: características mais importantes para decidir não votar em um candidato a presidente — Foto: Arte/g1

No gráfico abaixo, veja as respostas considerando o posicionamento político dos entrevistados.

Quaest: característica mais importante para não votar para presidente por identificação política — Foto: Arte/g1

A Quaest entrevistou 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais em todo o país, entre os dias 30 de agosto e 1º de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa foi registrada no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) sob o número BR-07065/2026.

Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos e Romeu Zema — Foto: Globo

articles.title: From 'remigration' to home-schooling: what does Germany's AfD want?
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) was founded in response to the euro crisis, but its focus has shifted firmly to the far right. A stridently hardline anti-i...
articles.body:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) was founded in response to the euro crisis but has shifted its focus to the far right, with a stridently hardline anti-immigration stance as its signature issue.

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is polling above 40% ahead of an election, with plans to introduce segregated classes for asylum-seekers' children, ban rainbow flags in schools, and cancel contracts with regional public broadcaster MDR among other controversial proposals.

The party's manifesto also includes commitments to allow home-schooling, block wind turbine construction, and set up a task force to speed up deportations, with potential tensions arising from its explicit backing of family structures based on marriage between a man and a woman.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) was founded in response to the euro crisis, but its focus has shifted firmly to the far right.

A stridently hardline anti-immigration stance, developed during the European migration crisis of 2015-16, is now the party's signature issue.

The AfD is seen to have profited from years of concern among many German voters over the huge numbers of refugees seeking asylum in the country from war-torn countries such as Syria and Ukraine.

Its manifesto at the last national election called for controls at the country's borders and "remigration," a term used in far-right circles to refer to the forced resettlement of certain immigrants.

Founded by eurosceptics in 2013, the party is highly critical of the European Union and believes in having nationalist pride in German history and culture. But the party did not explicitly call for withdrawal from the bloc in its 2025 Bundestag election manifesto.

On Russia, the AfD's position is widely seen as more pro-Kremlin than any mainstream party. The party has criticized the sanctions that have been imposed on Moscow for its war against Ukraine, calling for renewed purchases of Russian gas and an end to arms supplies to Kiev.

Like many parties, the AfD is not uniform and has various factions. The firebrand regional leader of the AfD in the eastern state of Thuringia, Björn Höcke, has been convicted for using a banned Nazi slogan.

In neighbouring Saxony-Anhalt, the party's lead candidate Siegmund strikes a more moderate tone, but its manifesto is highly controversial.

Ahead of Sunday's election, the AfD is polling above 40% and hoping to take control of a German state government for the first time in its history.

The party has outlined a 10-point plan of priorities for its first 100 days in office, committing to introduce segregated classes for the children of asylum-seekers, ban rainbow flags in schools, cancel contracts with regional public broadcaster MDR, cut a state ministry and set up a commission to investigate the response to the coronavirus pandemic.

Other commitments include allowing children to be home-schooled, blocking the construction of wind turbines, and setting up a task force to speed up deportations.

The Saxony-Anhalt manifesto also explicitly backs family structures based on marriage between a man and a woman, exposing tensions between the state and national party, whose co-leader Alice Weidel is in a same-sex relationship.

The AfD's policies would have a real impact on the daily lives of the state's 2.1 million residents, but how many of them can actually be achieved in the face of likely opposition in the courts and the federal government remains to be seen.

In Germany's federal system, state governments wield significant powers over health care, education, cultural affairs and media, while the national government in Berlin retains exclusive power over foreign affairs, defence, federal taxes and, crucially, immigration.

articles.title: Ranking the Republican 2028 contenders
articles.summary: President Trump dominates the political landscape, holding off lame-duck status for now. But some signs are emerging that prominent members of his party are readying 2028 presidential bids. Those moves are only likely to accelerate after November’s midterms. A post-Trump landscape will be tricky to navigate. The president has transformed his party during his decade…
articles.body:
President Trump dominates the political landscape, holding off lame-duck status for now.

But some signs are emerging that prominent members of his party are readying 2028 presidential bids. Those moves are only likely to accelerate after November’s midterms.

A post-Trump landscape will be tricky to navigate. The president has transformed his party during his decade in political life, shifting its policy positions on topics from immigration to trade, and transforming the tenor in which it conducts debate.

One big question for Republican primary voters in 2028 is whether they would prefer a nominee who tries to replicate Trump’s approach or one who seeks to write a new page.

There are plenty of options — assuming, of course, that Trump does not find a pretext to seek a third term. This is prohibited by any normal reading of the Constitution. Even Trump seems to — mostly — acknowledge it’s not possible.

Vice President Vance is the obvious heir apparent — as any vice president so much younger than the commander in chief would be.

Vance, 42, has always had a lot of backing within Trump’s inner circle, which helped him to be chosen as the president’s 2024 running mate in the first place.

Vance is also seen by the Make America Great Again (MAGA) grassroots as one of their own.

This, admittedly, rather whitewashes Vance’s history, which includes once wondering to a friend if Trump could be “America’s Hitler.”

He has long disavowed his earlier criticism, however, and has been a loyal deputy to Trump. He is a fervent believer in the president’s right-wing populist message.

Vance is also known to have been more skeptical than other senior figures in the administration about the decision to go to war in Iran. His perceived reluctance could be a political asset, given the unpopularity of the war with the public at large.

All of that being said, almost nobody believes Vance is a shoo-in for the nomination. It’s not clear Trump would endorse him. More broadly there are questions about Vance’s political skill while other critics see him as lacking in charisma.

His showing in his only run for elected office was solid but unspectacular: He won a U.S. Senate seat representing his native Ohio by 7 points in 2022.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vance are, by almost universal agreement, the two front-runners for the 2028 nomination.

In an Emerson College poll for The Hill last month, the secretary of State ran mostly better than Vance in hypothetical match-ups against several potential Democratic nominees.

Rubio has been in the national spotlight since 2010 when he won a U.S. Senate seat representing Florida.

His experience has made him a more fluent political performer than Vance. Earlier this year, when each man took a turn at the lectern of the White House briefing room during then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s maternity leave, Rubio appeared to earn more praise.

The son of Cuban immigrants, Rubio is known for his longstanding desire to remove the regime that has been in place on the island since the late Fidel Castro led his revolutionary forces to victory in 1959.

Rubio was enthused about the U.S. operation that seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro at the start of this year, and he has similarly hawkish views on Iran.

As such, he could position himself as something of a bridge between Trump’s “America First” supporters and the GOP’s more traditional wing on foreign affairs.

There are, however, questions of authenticity that have long floated around Rubio.

He was also a harsh critic of Trump when he ran against him for the 2016 GOP nomination. The campaign may seem like ancient history now, but it would be excavated for attack ads by rival candidates if Rubio went forward with a 2028 bid.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is one of the few figures outside Trump’s inner circle who could pose a real threat to Vance and Rubio. He is making little secret of the fact that he will probably try.

In a recent interview with MS NOW, Cruz pushed back against the idea that the GOP was beginning to coalesce around Vance as its likely nominee.

When it came to the question of where the Republican Party was going and what its identity should be, Cruz stated that he would be “ part of the discussion .”

Cruz, 55, is vigorously conservative, and his base in Texas gives him strong relationships with many big GOP donors.

Like Rubio, Cruz ran against Trump in 2016 before going on to make his peace with the president.

Even so, he can sometimes at least hint at criticism. In the MS NOW interview, he lauded Trump as a an “extraordinary” and “ferocious” figure but added: “I wish sometimes there was more message discipline and focus.”

Plenty of Republicans feel the same way. A Cruz campaign would be an intriguing test of how many of them the Texas senator could convert into supporters.

Among serious contenders, few divide opinion as much as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

His advocates point to his electoral successes in Florida, his embrace of the president’s agenda especially in terms of immigration and opposition to supposed “wokeness,” and the clout that comes from being governor of a large, increasingly Republican state.

But DeSantis’s downsides are equally obvious. His 2024 campaign against Trump never fired on all cylinders. It did, however, mark the Florida governor as a figure of suspicion in the minds of many Trump supporters.

While Vance, Rubio and Cruz are all assumed to be likely to run in 2028, that is less true of DeSantis, for whom the 2024 campaign was a bruising experience.

Could the ardor that the GOP base feels for the current president be transferred to his eldest son?

The younger Trump has never run for office. Then again, neither had his father prior to 2016.

First, the younger Trump makes news these days primarily because of business interests that have been deeply controversial. The sums of money involved are often vast.

To take just one example, in July The Washington Post reported that “a portfolio of defense technology start-ups” in which Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump have invested “have collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business.”

Second, many doubt whether the force of his last name alone could propel Trump Jr. — a somewhat socially awkward figure not known for achievements outside the family — to the same political heights as his father.

One of the most intriguing — and controversial — prospects within the GOP is the idea of a presidential run by the conservative commentator.

Tucker Carlson, who was once a staunch backer of Trump, has turned against him, primarily over the war in Iran. The former Fox News host has also become a fervent critic of Israel and its influence on American foreign policy.

To his fans, Carlson has remained true to the populist, “America First” ideology that they believe Trump was supposed to represent. To his detractors, he is stoking his own notoriety by attacking the president and giving a platform to fringe extremists.

Carlson has suggested he won’t run for president, but a livestream last month in which he outlined a 10-point manifesto hardly tamped down the speculation.

He has also become strongly critical of the GOP itself, which appears to make a third-party bid more likely than a tilt at the Republican nomination.

Late last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth emphatically denied an NBC News report that he had “told close friends and associates that he is considering a run for president in 2028.”

The secretary of Defense wrote on social media that the story was “100% false.”

Beyond the specifics of that story, a 2028 run doesn’t seem beyond the bounds of possibility for the ambitious former TV host.

But his tenure at the Pentagon has been deeply controversial, even among some Republicans.

The recent departure of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll was one more data point fueling skepticism about Hegseth’s overall approach.

Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) appeal is somewhat similar to that of Cruz, except the Arkansas senator is a few years younger and unencumbered by the baggage of a previous run for the presidency.

Cotton, 49, is just as firmly conservative and a good communicator who keeps his profile high with regular appearances in friendly media.

Cotton faces the perennial problem for candidates who are seen as outside the top tier, however.

It’s hard to see him outflanking everyone to actually become the nominee, though it’s quite easy to see him as a possible vice presidential pick.

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders still has a reservoir of support among Trump fans because of her stint as White House press secretary during his first term.

She won election as governor of her native Arkansas in 2022 and is up for reelection this year. One recent poll had her leading only by a surprisingly narrow 5-point margin, but it would be a huge shock if she were to lose.

Sanders hasn’t said much about a possible 2028 bid, though she does have a book coming out this fall, which will see her step more firmly into the national spotlight.

Right now, she appears to be the only viable female candidate for the GOP nomination in 2028.

As a two-term governor of a large Southern state, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp looks good on paper. He will soon have time on his hands to focus on a presidential bid as well: Term limits prevent him from seeking reelection this year.

The big problem for Kemp is his complicated and sometimes rancorous relationship with Trump.

For Kemp to become the nominee, the GOP would have to be ready to rebuke Trump and Trumpism. There is vanishingly little evidence that it is.

articles.title: House Dems plot Trump investigation blitz if they seize majority
articles.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia outlined key targets, including the Trump family, Jeffrey Epstein and ICE, as House Democrats prepare oversight investigations.
articles.body: House Democrats are planning for a slew of investigations targeting President Donald Trump, his Cabinet, and his family if they win the midterm elections. In just two months, voters across the country will decide which party controls Congress for the second half of President Donald Trump's final term. Historical trends dictate that the party in power in the White House — in this case, Republicans — usually loses one or both chambers. Democrats in the House of Representatives are already planning for that eventuality, key left-wing leaders told Fox News Digital. SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS "I'm going to start on the Department of Defense. Our service members are being put at tremendous risk. There is corruption, there's incompetence, there is nepotism at the DoD," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told Fox News Digital. "There are very disturbing reports about ties between defense money and appropriations programs, and requests by the White House to funnel defense spending to certain companies linked to the Trump family. So we're going to take a hard look at all of that." 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN Crow sits on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees, in addition to co-chairing the House Anti-Corruption Caucus. He was also notably one of the impeachment managers who helped lead one of two pushes by Democrats to keep Trump out of power. Asked if impeachment could pop up again — whether for Trump or his appointees — Crow did not rule it out. GOP LAWMAKER UNVEILS HISTORIC MOVE TO 'EXPUNGE' BOTH 'MALICIOUSLY FALSE' IMPEACHMENTS AGAINST TRUMP "It's one of several tools that Congress has to pursue accountability, to get information, and to attack corruption," Crow said. "I won't hesitate to use that tool if that's the right one. But there are other tools available to us, too." Several impeachment resolutions have been introduced over the last two years targeting both Trump and his officials, but none have gained steam within the wider Democratic Caucus. HOUSE DEMS UNVEIL BILL TO EXAMINE REMOVING TRUMP USING 25TH AMENDMENT House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has demurred on multiple occasions when asked about impeachment. And it likely won't be the first tool in Democrats' arsenal that they'd wield if they win in November, two of their presumptive chairmen suggested. The most likely first approach will be tackling what Democrats see as corruption and mismanagement of federal agencies. JEFFRIES' REPORTED MEETING WITH KUSHNER ABOUT POSSIBLE TRUMP COOPERATION DRAWS LEFT-WING BACKLASH Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to take over the House Oversight Committee if the chamber flips, told reporters he was already working closely with presumptive House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jamie Raskin, D-Md., on potential investigations. Garcia told Fox News Digital there were "a few key investigations" he was already looking at. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING "One is going to be the Trump family corruption. The second will be the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Third will be ICE and DHS and the corruption happening there," Garcia said. "We'll also go into anyone that's ripping off the American public from a corporate perspective or CEO perspective. And then lastly, there's a lot of interest in the committee on taking on what's happening to the destruction of our vaccination process and [Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr.]." Raskin, meanwhile, has already previewed what his panel's investigations would look like. He's sent a flurry of requests for information targeting the business dealings of Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as well as Donald Trump Jr. and FBI Director Kash Patel, among others. TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS "The Trump family has turned the entire executive branch into a money-making enterprise, so there’s more than enough corruption and lawlessness to keep Democrats across the House busy for years. Judiciary Democrats are already following the evidence wherever it leads, from the Trump family’s astonishing self-dealing and conflicts of interest to the corporations and law firms that have colluded with this administration for profit, advantage and protection," Raskin told Fox News Digital when asked about his plans. "We will continue to work together across committees and use every investigative and legislative tool we have to uncover the facts, expose the wrongdoing and its costs for the public, hold the perpetrators and profiteers accountable, and pass legislative cures." Republicans have long feared that Democrats winning either the House or Senate will grind the GOP's agenda to a halt in Washington. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., previously told Fox News Digital that he believed Democrats would try to impeach Trump "on Day 1" if they win. Trump, meanwhile, has maintained his innocence amid an array of accusations from the left. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Trump's ballroom win highlights need for serious judicial nominees
articles.summary: The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling on the White House ballroom lawsuit exposes deep rifts, with Chief Justice John Roberts penning a sharp dissent.
articles.body: Last year, President Trump ordered construction of a White House ballroom and a secure underground military facility. A DC busybody sued to stop it, and on Aug. 31, the Supreme Court killed this laughable lawsuit by a single vote. Mid-construction, long after the East Wing’s demolition, Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three Democrat women to try to shut down the president of the United States’ security improvement, expressly permitted by federal statute and Article II of the Constitution, to the White House complex. This narrow 5-4 ruling proves precisely why Republicans must continue to nominate and confirm rock-solid constitutionalists all across the federal judiciary. For decades, the White House hosted large events in outdoor tents, with women’s high heels sinking into the soggy Rose Garden and other White House grounds. But that open setting provides a rich target for terrorists, including too many of today’s Democrats, who wish to harm the president. The threat is all too real. Just over two years ago, Matthew Thomas Crooks nearly assassinated Trump at an open-air campaign rally in Butler, Pa. Two months later, Ryan Routh attempted another assassination of Trump at a Florida golf course. In April, a third would-be assassin attempted to murder Trump in a DC hotel ballroom at the annual White House Correspondents’ Dinner. The dire need for a highly secure White House ballroom is obvious—and presidents and their guests long after Trump will enjoy its beauty, utility, and convenience. The White House regularly hosts heads of state, members of Congress, foreign diplomats, and other high-value targets of America’s enemies. Any reasonable person ought to know that, in these disturbing times, we need the most enhanced security imaginable. Trump acted. He ordered the demolition of the run-down, long-past-its-prime White House East Wing to build a privately funded, 70-foot-tall indoor ballroom, a subterranean military bunker, and rooftop security facility. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL Enter Alison Hoagland, an underworked DC busybody and member of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who claims she leisurely strolls by the White House vicinity about once a month —while real Americans, in real America, work real jobs. She filed suit, claiming the new ballroom was unsightly and offended her apparently very delicate aesthetic sensibilities. DC U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee who suffers from severe Trump Derangement Syndrome like so many other Republican-appointed DC federal judges, took the bait. He blocked all new above-ground construction for the East Wing unless the subsurface military facility strictly required it. APPEALS COURT LETS TRUMP RESUME WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION, SEEKS LOWER COURT CLARITY DC federal judges are legendary for their self-imagined expertise in . . . well, everything. But a judge who has never had a real job in his adult life deluding himself into believing his job is now to moonlight as the construction foreman over the White House complex, instead of the duly-elected president of the United States (who happens to be one of the best builders in the world for over 50 years), is next-level judicial narcissism and lawlessness. Unsurprisingly, the Democrat-dominated DC Circuit upheld Leon’s rogue ruling over a superb dissent by U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a former law clerk to America’s all-time-greatest Justice Clarence Thomas. The Trump administration took the fight to the Supreme Court, as these DC federal courts would turn the White House complex into a stop-work construction site for years. TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT Article III of the U.S. Constitution requires a plaintiff to have standing. In order to bring suit in federal court, a plaintiff needs a concrete, redressable injury that has already occurred or which imminently looms. Plaintiff/DC busybody Alison Hoagland had nothing but her hurt feelings. The High Court has never held that mere personal offense gives someone the right to bring a federal case. Five of the six Republican-appointed Supreme Court justices correctly rejected Hoagland’s crackpot standing claim. Ruling for her would let anyone file a lawsuit to stop any government building project in America based on aesthetics and hurt feelings. The majority also torched Leon’s unworkable injunction. Leon, the self-appointed construction foreman as even former U.S. Attorney General William Barr —certainly no Trump cheerleader —mocked him , demanded the White House prove every foot of the project served a critical purpose, a subjective standard that would require endless court appearances, construction delays for years, and unnecessary security risks at the White House complex. Yet Chief Justice John Roberts ignored this basic logic and decided to pen a truly cringeworthy dissent. He argued standing depends on whether a government building is "iconic." He cherry-picked a century-old quote from Theodore Roosevelt to invent a limitless theory of standing. This ludicrous view came within one vote of prevailing. There must be something in the water in these DC federal courthouses. Earlier this year, Leon enjoined lawful sanctions against Francesca Albanese, the International Criminal Court’s head prosecutor. The ICC had issued an absurd arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump rightfully sanctioned the ICC and its officials. But that didn’t faze Leon. Leon protected Albanese simply because her husband and children hold American citizenship. Thankfully, a D.C. Circuit panel stayed Leon’s stunning injunction, and the sanctions against Albanese remain in effect. TRUMP SUFFERS MAJOR SUPREME COURT DEFEAT AS JUSTICES UPHOLD BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP Roberts’ record is even worse. He cast the deciding vote to uphold Obamacare in 2012, killed the first Trump administration’s U.S. Census citizenship question in 2020, and protected DACA in 2020. He penned a gratuitous concurrence in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), explicitly noting he was not voting to overturn Roe v. Wade (1973), one of the worst decisions in Supreme Court history. This June, Roberts delivered his coup de grâce. He authored Trump v. Barbara, an egregiously wrong opinion constitutionalizing birthright citizenship for the children of illegal immigrants–including 1.5 million (and growing) Chinese birth tourists. Roberts' ruling is the gravest betrayal of our most crucial sovereign power as We The People, the sovereign citizens of America: to control who becomes one of us. Yet Roberts’ ballroom dissent read like a fever dream, following a bad bout of Trump Derangement Syndrome. JUSTICE THOMAS WARNS PROGRESSIVISM IS A THREAT TO AMERICA IN RARE PUBLIC REMARKS It could have been worse. Bush put former U.S. Circuit Judge J. Michael Luttig on his Supreme Court short list. This is the same Luttig who advocated throwing Trump off the 2024 ballot under the preposterous theory that he committed "insurrection" on Jan. 6, 2021. That ludicrous argument ultimately didn’t garner a single vote at the Supreme Court—not even from the three Democrat women who generally rule against Trump after simply seeing his name in the case caption. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Article III Project proudly stands with Trump. We demand staunch constitutionalists in the mold of Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito. Decades of spineless Republican judges—particularly in the DC swamp--have severely damaged this nation, and the Article III Project will lead the fight to ensure those days never return. Bold and fearless constitutionalists in the mold of new Trump-appointed U.S. Circuit Judge Emil Bove is our future. We won’t get fooled again.
